source: In a fair test you change only one thing, keep everything else the same, and measure what happens. Then you can tell what made the difference.
Changing two things at once (more water and more sun) and then not knowing which one helped the plant grow.

Sam wants to know if plant food helps bean plants grow. He gives one plant food and leaves one without. But he also puts the fed plant in the sunny window and the other in a dark corner. When the fed plant grows taller, what made the difference?
He cannot tell! He changed two things at once: the food and the light.
In a fair test you change only one thing (the thing you are testing), keep everything else the same, and measure the result. Do it more than once to be sure.
A fair test: same pots, same soil, same water and the same sunny window. Only the plant food was different.
Lily tests which ball bounces higher. She drops the red ball from her waist and the blue ball from over her head.
Not fair. Drop both balls from the same height onto the same floor.
She is testing the ball, so only the ball should change.
But the drop height changed too, and a higher drop makes a higher bounce.
Changing two things at once, or testing only one time. One plant can be sick by bad luck; three plants each way gives a fairer answer.
Going further. In the Pendulums lab, change only the length, then only the weight, and see which one changes the swing.
